# R3 Digest — Weima BECNT 1 Thess 2:17–3:13

**Source:** Jeffrey A. Weima, *1–2 Thessalonians* (BECNT)  
**Exclusive range:** original lines **2973–3417** (slice file lines 1–445)  
**Scope:** III.B Defense of Present Absence from Thessalonica (2:17–3:10) + III.C Transitional Prayers (3:11–13)  
**Extractor role:** claims/digest only; no wiki page edits  
**Attribution:** all interpretive claims are **Weima’s** (or Weima reporting secondary scholarship); not bare wiki voice

---

## Claims

### C1 — Twin concerns of 2:17–3:10
- **Locus:** §B intro (slice ~L1–6)
- **Quote:** “Paul addresses two closely connected concerns stemming from his present absence… The apostle is concerned first that his inability to return… might be used by opponents… to raise further doubts… Paul responds in 2:17–20… by employing the apostolic parousia… The apostle is concerned, second, about the persecution that threatens the faith… In 3:1–5 Paul responds… by referring to the sending of his emissary Timothy… These two concerns are skillfully combined and answered in 3:6–10.”
- **Claim:** Weima frames 2:17–3:10 as answering (1) doubt over Paul’s love due to absence (via apostolic parousia) and (2) threat to the church’s faith under persecution (via Timothy’s mission), both resolved in Timothy’s return-report.
- **Targets:** `1-thessalonians`, `jeffrey-weima`, `paul-apostle`, `timothy`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C2 — Apostolic parousia as form of 2:17–3:10
- **Locus:** Literary Analysis / Character (slice ~L12–19)
- **Quote:** “1 Thess. 2:17–3:10 ought to be identified as an ‘apostolic parousia,’ that is, a section of the letter where Paul is particularly concerned to make his ‘presence’ (the Greek word παρουσία [parousia] has not only the sense of ‘coming, arrival’ but also ‘presence’) more powerfully experienced by the readers.”
- **Claim:** Weima identifies the unit as apostolic parousia (presence-device), citing Funk, White, Boers, Aune, Jervis, Trebilco; notes parousia = coming/arrival *and* presence.
- **Targets:** `1-thessalonians`, `parousia-1-thess-4`, `jeffrey-weima`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C3 — Loose topos, not rigid five-unit form
- **Locus:** Form discussion (slice ~L14–19)
- **Quote:** “The difficulty with both these formal analyses is that the parallels… are not great enough to warrant the identification of specific units and subunits. It is better… to speak of the apostolic parousia as a distinct epistolary convention that exhibits a rather loose form… As Aune… states: ‘The absence of a consistent structure… suggests that we are dealing with a topos or theme with a number of subordinate motifs.’”
- **Claim:** Weima prefers Aune’s “topos/theme with subordinate motifs” over Funk’s five major units or Jervis’s three functional units (Letter Writing / Sending of Emissary / Apostolic Visit).
- **Targets:** `jeffrey-weima`, `1-thessalonians`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C4 — Function in 1 Thess: love/reassurance, not primarily authority
- **Locus:** Function (slice ~L20–28)
- **Quote:** “The function of the apostolic parousia in 1 Thess. 2:17–3:10… differs slightly from that found elsewhere… Here the apostle makes his parousia… more strongly experienced… not so much to exert his authority as to reassure them of his continued love and care for them. As Jervis… concludes… ‘Thus the dominant function of the apostolic parousia of 1 Thessalonians is to express Paul’s love for his Thessalonian converts and to encourage them in their faith.’”
- **Claim:** Weima (with Jervis) argues that here the device primarily reassures love and removes uncertainty over non-return, not authority-enforcement (contrast Romans 15; Philem. 22).
- **Targets:** `paul-apostle`, `1-thessalonians`, `jeffrey-weima`

### C5 — Apostolic parousia prepares for paraenesis (4:1–5:22)
- **Locus:** Function, larger letter (slice ~L28–29)
- **Quote:** “As with the apostolic apology in 2:1–16, so also the apostolic parousia here in 2:17–3:10 serves to reestablish the trust and confidence of Paul’s readers such that they will submit to the exhortative material (paraenesis) that follows in the second half of the letter (4:1–5:22).”
- **Claim:** Weima gives the unit a letter-wide function: rebuild trust so readers accept later exhortations.
- **Targets:** `1-thessalonians`, `jeffrey-weima`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C6 — Passage extent: 2:17–3:10 ends before 3:11–13
- **Locus:** Extent of the Passage (slice ~L31–51)
- **Quote:** “It is best, therefore, to treat 3:11–13 as an independent, transitional unit in the letter—one that not only echoes material in the first half… but also anticipates the issues to be developed in the second half.”
- **Claim:** Against Rigaux/Best/Bruce et al., Weima (with Lightfoot, Milligan, Frame, Wanamaker, Holmstrand, Malherbe) separates 2:17–3:10 (apostolic parousia) from 3:11–13 (two prayers/benedictions), citing formal difference, inclusios (face/heart + face-to-face; joy; faith leitmotif absent from prayers).
- **Targets:** `1-thessalonians`, `jeffrey-weima`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C7 — Three-unit structure of 2:17–3:10
- **Locus:** Structure (slice ~L53–76)
- **Quote:** “2:17–3:10 consists of three distinct units: 2:17–20; 3:1–5; and 3:6–10… 1. Paul’s concern over his absence… 2. Paul’s concern over the persecution… 3. Both concerns answered: Timothy’s ‘good news’…”
- **Claim:** Weima outlines (1) absence 2:17–20, (2) persecution 3:1–5 (inclusio 3:1–2 // 3:5), (3) both answered 3:6–10; same Satanic power behind absence (2:18) and temptation (3:5).
- **Targets:** `1-thessalonians`, `timothy`, `paul-apostle`, `jeffrey-weima`

### C8 — “Orphaned”: Paul as orphaned child, not bereft parent
- **Locus:** [2:17] (slice ~L96–100)
- **Quote:** “By employing the verbal form aporphanisthentes, Paul presents himself and his coworkers as children whose forced departure from Thessalonica has meant that they are orphaned from the believers in that city… it never refers to parents who are orphaned from their children but always refers to children who are orphaned from their parents… Paul wrenches the metaphor to extract the most emotion possible from it.”
- **Claim:** Weima (citing Faulkenberry Miller; Chrysostom; Malherbe) insists ἀπορφανισθέντες depicts **Paul and coworkers as orphans**, not Thessalonians as orphans or Paul as orphaned father; many translations/commentators obscure this.
- **Targets:** `paul-apostle`, `1-thessalonians`, `jeffrey-weima`

### C9 — “Short time… face but not heart”; piled desire language
- **Locus:** [2:17] (slice ~L102–110)
- **Quote:** “for a short time, in person but not in heart”… “Paul has apparently created this striking phrase… to stress that his absence is for a limited rather than indefinite or permanent time… ‘We most earnestly made every effort to see you face-to-face with great desire’… σπουδάζειν indicates more than mere desire; it denotes actual effort… Here… epithymia… in the positive sense of ‘desire.’”
- **Claim:** Weima reads 2:17 as minimizing permanence (pros kairon hōras), asserting heart-presence, and hyperbolically stacking perissoterōs + spoudazō + pollē epithymia to show intense longing and effort.
- **Targets:** `paul-apostle`, `1-thessalonians`

### C10 — Personal interjection; “more than once”; Satan blocked the way
- **Locus:** [2:18] (slice ~L112–119)
- **Quote:** “In fact, I, Paul, wanted to do so more than once—but Satan blocked our way… hapax kai dis… denotes a plurality of occasions (two or more)… The verb ἐγκόπτω… derives… from ‘the military practice of making slits in the road…’ Hence the basic meaning is ‘to block the way’… later prayer of 3:11… ‘May God himself… clear the way…’”
- **Claim:** Weima stresses personalized Paul-interjection; hapax kai dis = multiple attempts not exactly two; Satan’s hindrance is military road-blocking metaphor that 3:11 answers; specific historical means remain unspecified speculation (Jewish plots, politarch security, illness, etc.).
- **Targets:** `paul-apostle`, `1-thessalonians`, `jeffrey-weima`

### C11 — “Satan”: theological interpretation, not mere excuse
- **Locus:** [2:18] (slice ~L120–122)
- **Quote:** “The name or title ‘Satan’ is a transliteration of the Hebrew… meaning ‘accuser’… Paul… theologically interprets the historical circumstances surrounding his inability to revisit the Thessalonians as the work of Satan… should not be cynically dismissed as merely a ploy… he is also surely reflecting his genuine conviction.”
- **Claim:** Weima catalogs Pauline Satan titles (including “the Tempter” 3:5) and insists 2:18 is both persuasive rhetoric and sincere apocalyptic worldview.
- **Targets:** `paul-apostle`, `1-thessalonians`, `jeffrey-weima`

### C12 — Hope, joy, crown of boasting at the Lord’s parousia
- **Locus:** [2:19–20] (slice ~L124–146)
- **Quote:** “For who is our hope and joy and crown of boasting—Is it not, in fact, you?—before our Lord Jesus at his coming?… juridical context… the Thessalonian congregation will be the proof he will present before the returning Jesus… crown of boasting… from the Hellenistic athletic contests where the victor received a wreath… not a false boasting… but a vindicating note of exultation for the work… that God brought about through him… ‘For you are our pride and joy.’”
- **Claim:** Weima reads the triad as eschatological-juridical: Thessalonians as evidence of faithful apostleship at Christ’s parousia; stephanos = athletic wreath (not diadem); doxa = “pride/fame” not religious “glory”; present-tense este: they already are pride and joy.
- **Targets:** `1-thessalonians`, `parousia-1-thess-4`, `paul-apostle`, `jeffrey-weima`

### C13 — Parousia term: Hellenistic royal visit + OT roots
- **Locus:** [2:19] (slice ~L140–142)
- **Quote:** “When the apostle uses this term to refer to Jesus… it always refers to his ‘coming’… In the Hellenistic world… parousia was a technical term that referred… more commonly, the coming of kings or high-ranking leaders… to a city for an official visit… Despite these OT roots… the predominately Gentile church of Thessalonica would naturally have understood the parousia in terms of the royal visits of the Roman emperors… may well explain… ‘saying that there is another king, Jesus’ (Acts 17:7).”
- **Claim:** Weima’s technical sketch of parousia (presence/coming; royal visit; OT day of the Lord roots; Gentile political hearing; possible reason for later vocabulary shifts).
- **Targets:** `parousia-1-thess-4`, `1-thessalonians`, `jeffrey-weima`

### C14 — 3:1–5: persecution concern within apostolic parousia via Timothy
- **Locus:** §2 intro (slice ~L149–152)
- **Quote:** “Although Paul is not able to be with them in person, he continues to make his presence among them more powerfully felt (the apostolic parousia) by referring to the sending of his emissary, Timothy.”
- **Claim:** Weima ties persecution unit to same parousia strategy: emissary-sending as alternate presence medium.
- **Targets:** `timothy`, `paul-apostle`, `1-thessalonians`

### C15 — “Could no longer contain it”; left alone in Athens
- **Locus:** [3:1] (slice ~L154–160)
- **Quote:** “because we could no longer contain it, we thought it best to be left behind in Athens alone… στέγω… ‘at the core of its meaning στέγω denotes an activity or state which blocks entry from without or exit from within’… he is no longer able to prevent his strong emotions for them from leaking out… eudokēsamen expresses not joy… but resolve.”
- **Claim:** Weima’s stegō image = emotions “leaking”; monoi/left-behind stresses loneliness echoing orphan metaphor; resolve not happiness at solitude.
- **Targets:** `paul-apostle`, `1-thessalonians`, `timothy`

### C16 — Literary plural “we”; sequence with Acts (Timothy from Athens)
- **Locus:** [3:1] movements reconstruction (slice ~L160–169)
- **Quote:** “Most commentators… view the ‘we’ in 3:1 as a literary or epistolary plural: Paul was left behind in Athens by himself… After his two coworkers return to him in Athens, Paul sends Timothy back to Thessalonica… The apostle also sends Silas away… Timothy returns to Paul… who by this time has left Athens to begin an eighteen-month ministry in Corinth (Acts 18:1–17)… return of both Timothy and Silas from Macedonia (Acts 18:5).”
- **Claim:** Weima takes “we” as literary plural; reconstructs: Athens reunion → Timothy to Thessalonica (Silas likely Macedonia/Philippi gifts) → Timothy/Silas rejoin Paul in Corinth → report prompts 1 Thessalonians.
- **Targets:** `paul-apostle`, `timothy`, `silas`, `1-thessalonians`, `jeffrey-weima`

### C17 — Timothy: “brother and coworker of God”; authoritative emissary
- **Locus:** [3:2] + Additional Notes (slice ~L171–176, ~L289–303)
- **Quote:** “we sent Timothy, our brother and coworker of God in the gospel of Christ… both titles have the function of stressing the authoritative status of Timothy: he is no mere mailman… but an authoritative coworker of both Paul and even God… First… most difficult reading… ‘coworker of God’… best explains the rise of the other four readings.”
- **Claim:** Weima prefers συνεργὸν τοῦ θεοῦ; titles confer authority so Paul’s absence is mitigated by high-status proxy; possible reason Timothy sent: not named in Acts 17 legal ban/security deposit.
- **Targets:** `timothy`, `paul-apostle`, `jeffrey-weima`, `1-thessalonians`

### C18 — Purpose of Timothy’s mission: strengthen and comfort faith
- **Locus:** [3:2] (slice ~L178–182)
- **Quote:** “in order to strengthen you and comfort you concerning your faith… stērixai… ‘confirm, establish, strengthen’… contrast the danger of being ‘shaken’… parakalesai… more pastoral sense of comfort… ‘faith’… refers… to a whole range of Christian activities that result from their faith in God.”
- **Claim:** Twin purpose infinitives (strengthen/comfort) aim at pisteis under persecution; faith = broad lived faith, key term five times in 3:2–10.
- **Targets:** `timothy`, `1-thessalonians`, `jeffrey-weima`

### C19 — “Not shaken by these afflictions”; external persecution, not mere inward anxiety
- **Locus:** [3:3a] (slice ~L184–193)
- **Quote:** “so that no one may be shaken by these afflictions… second and more probable meaning… ‘to cause to be emotionally upset, move, disturb, agitate’… It would be wrong… to limit the thlipsesin… as inward anxieties… external opposition likely involved severe social harassment and ostracism rather than physical death… primarily… afflictions that the Thessalonians were enduring.”
- **Claim:** Weima rejects “flatter” sense of sainesthai and Malherbe/Richard inward-anxiety narrowing of thlipsis; primary referent is Thessalonians’ outward social hostility (2:14).
- **Targets:** `1-thessalonians`, `jeffrey-weima`, `paul-apostle`

### C20 — Destined for affliction; prophecy-fulfillment; inclusive “we”
- **Locus:** [3:3b–4] (slice ~L195–204)
- **Quote:** “For you yourselves know that we are destined for this… ‘Normality is persecution’… ‘We are destined to suffer affliction’… prophecy-fulfillment argument… inclusive ‘we’… antidote to any accusation… that the apostle’s ongoing absence… stems from a selfish desire… to avoid… suffering.”
- **Claim:** Weima stresses divine destiny of suffering (keimai + mellō thlibesthai), repeated pre-teaching, fulfilled and known; solidarity “we”; reestablishes credibility.
- **Targets:** `1-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`, `jeffrey-weima`

### C21 — Inclusio 3:5; the Tempter; work “in vain”
- **Locus:** [3:5] (slice ~L206–221)
- **Quote:** “because I could no longer contain it, I sent in order to learn about your faith, fearing that in some way the Tempter had tempted you and that our work might have been in vain… epeirasen… indicative… certainty that the Tempter had indeed been at work… genētai… subjunctive… uncertainty about the outcome… same evil, supernatural figure… agents of Satan… ‘empty of result, in vain.’”
- **Claim:** Weima: singular intensifies personal concern; mission shifts slightly from equipping (3:2) to fact-finding (3:5); Tempter = Satan of 2:18; afflictions theologically framed as cosmic conflict; perseverance/election tension noted without full resolution; obligation rhetoric (not “in vain”).
- **Targets:** `1-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`, `timothy`, `jeffrey-weima`

### C22 — Timothy’s good news: faith and love answer both concerns
- **Locus:** [3:6] (slice ~L226–240)
- **Quote:** “Timothy has now come to us from you and has brought good news about your faith and love and that you have a good remembrance of us always, longing to see us just as we also long to see you… only nontechnical use in Paul [of euangelizō]… ‘faith’… answers… 3:1–5… ‘love’… almost certainly refers specifically to the Thessalonians’ continued affection for Paul… This looks like an apology for his failure to return.”
- **Claim:** Weima: euangelizō stresses thankfulness; faith ↔ persecution concern; love + good remembrance + mutual longing ↔ absence concern; against Malherbe’s non-apologetic reading, Weima sees defensive/apologetic force (with Frame, Best, Wanamaker on 3:6).
- **Targets:** `timothy`, `paul-apostle`, `1-thessalonians`, `jeffrey-weima`

### C23 — Comforted through their faith amid Paul’s distress and affliction
- **Locus:** [3:7] (slice ~L242–250)
- **Quote:** “we were comforted, brothers, because of you in all our distress and affliction through this faith of yours… reciprocal comfort… external opposition… past problems in Berea… alone… Athens… especially the current opposition… in Corinth… another fulfillment of his repeated prophecy.”
- **Claim:** Weima: eph’ hymin = causal “because of you”; anankē/thlipsis general hardships of ministry (esp. Corinth), not only separation-anguish; their faith is means of his comfort; solidarity and credibility themes continue.
- **Targets:** `paul-apostle`, `1-thessalonians`, `timothy`

### C24 — “Now we live, if you continue to stand firm in the Lord”
- **Locus:** [3:8] (slice ~L252–261)
- **Quote:** “For now we live, if you continue to stand firm in the Lord… hyperbolic expression… ean with the indicative… deliberate… hortatory quality… ‘stand firm in the Lord’… antidote… ‘not be shaken by these afflictions’… rely… in the one… able to deliver them from the wrath to come (1:10).”
- **Claim:** Weima: nun/arti chronological shift past fear → present life-as-hyperbole; ean + indicative = soft condition/exhortation not pure confidence; stēkō figurative steadfastness “in the Lord.”
- **Targets:** `1-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`, `jeffrey-weima`

### C25 — Night-and-day pleading; face-to-face and complete what lacks in faith
- **Locus:** [3:9–10] (slice ~L263–288)
- **Quote:** “What thanksgiving, then, can we pay back to God… because of all the joy… pleading night and day as earnestly as possible in order to see you face-to-face and complete the things that are lacking in your faith… hyperekperissou… ‘highest form of comparison imaginable’… first desire… inclusio with… 2:17… second… looks ahead to the rest of the letter… not specifically to a lack of eschatological hope but more generally to a variety of concerns… 4:1–5:22… not so great as to imply blame… or to negate… thanksgiving and praise.”
- **Claim:** Weima: thanksgiving to God (not them) for joy; deomai + night/day + hyperekperissou = intense frequent pleading; double purpose joins both unit concerns and anticipates paraenesis; rejects missing-hope-from-triad-silence reading; hysterēmata + katartisai imply real deficiencies without heavy culpability.
- **Targets:** `1-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`, `jeffrey-weima`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### C26 — 3:11–13 as transitional body benedictions/wish-prayers
- **Locus:** C. Transitional Prayers intro + Literary Analysis (slice ~L326–346)
- **Quote:** “The two prayers of 3:11–13 not only summarize the two major concerns developed in the first half of the letter but also foreshadow three key themes… transitional prayers… formally identified as ‘benedictions’… or ‘wish-prayers’… ‘body’ benediction… five basic elements… In fact, the emphasis… is less on the apologetic concerns… than on the exhortative concerns in the second half.”
- **Claim:** Weima classifies two body benedictions (3:11; 3:12–13), summarizing absence/persecution and foreshadowing love, holiness, parousia; paraenetic function via public prayer; not merely “concluding prayers.”
- **Targets:** `1-thessalonians`, `jeffrey-weima`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`, `parousia-1-thess-4`

### C27 — Unit boundaries of 3:11–13
- **Locus:** Extent (slice ~L347–350)
- **Quote:** “compelling grammatical and literary grounds… for beginning a new section in 3:11… contrastive particle δέ… change of subject… ‘our God and Father and our Lord Jesus’… shift… indicative to the optative… inclusio… ending… in 3:10… eschatological climax… ‘Amen’… clear new beginning in 4:1.”
- **Claim:** Weima rejects 3:9–13 as single prayer-unit; 3:11–13 is discrete, ends before 4:1.
- **Targets:** `1-thessalonians`, `jeffrey-weima`

### C28 — Prayer 1 (3:11): God and Lord Jesus clear the blocked way
- **Locus:** [3:11] (slice ~L370–386)
- **Quote:** “But may our God and Father himself and our Lord Jesus clear the way for us to come to you… slight adversative sense… over against… blocking work of Satan (2:18b)… two subjects… with a singular verb… suggests that Paul views Jesus as sharing the deity of God… kateuthynai… removal of the satanic obstacles… Satan has ‘blocked our way,’ but now God and Jesus will ‘clear our way to you.’”
- **Claim:** Weima: de + autos contrast ineffective human attempts with divine clearing; dual subject + singular verb neither pure Tritarianism-from-grammar-alone nor theologically insignificant—assumes Jesus’ divine status; optative = confident wish; kateuthynō answers 2:18 military road metaphor.
- **Targets:** `paul-apostle`, `1-thessalonians`, `jeffrey-weima`

### C29 — Prayer 2 (3:12): abounding love for one another and for all
- **Locus:** [3:12] (slice ~L389–404)
- **Quote:** “But as for you, may the Lord cause you to abound and increase in love for one another and for all, just as we also… ‘the Lord’… refers to Jesus… combination of pleonasai and perisseusai serves to intensify… love… anticipates… 4:9–12 and… 5:12–22… ‘and for all’… challenging… endure much affliction… elliptical phrase… echoes… concern… to reassure the Thessalonians of his continued love… ‘just as we also [long to see] you’ in 3:6.”
- **Claim:** Weima: emphatic hymas shifts object to church; Lord = Jesus; superlative growth in mutual and outsider love foreshadows 4:9–12 and 5:15; Pauline example clause reaffirms absence-defense love.
- **Targets:** `1-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`, `jeffrey-weima`

### C30 — Prayer purpose (3:13): strengthen hearts; blameless in holiness; parousia with holy ones
- **Locus:** [3:13] (slice ~L406–424)
- **Quote:** “in order to strengthen your hearts as blameless in holiness before our God and Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his holy ones… stērixai… recalls… sending Timothy… courage to stand firm… ‘blameless in holiness’… looks ahead to… 4:3–8… parousia… royal visit… ‘holy ones’… debate… angels or believers… Weima leans to believers/saints… every other… Paul… Christians… foreshadows… holiness… 4:3–8… ‘all’… anticipates… 4:13–18… deceased… will be present… Amen… slightly stronger evidence for… inclusion.”
- **Claim:** Weima: purpose looks back to strengthening under affliction and ahead to holiness (4:3–8) and eschatology (4:13–5:11); prefers hagioi = believers (with all living and dead at parousia), while surveying angel view (Zech 14:5; 2 Thess 1:7); reconciles with 4:14–17 via apantēsis escort imagery; favors including Amen.
- **Targets:** `1-thessalonians`, `parousia-1-thess-4`, `jeffrey-weima`, `paul-apostle`

### C31 — Text-critical notes of special load (2:19; 3:2; 3:8; 3:9; 3:13)
- **Locus:** Additional Notes (slice ~L288–313; ~L426–432)
- **Quote:** “Alexandrinus has replaced καυχήσεως… with ἀγαλλιάσεως… five different readings for… Timothy… first option [coworker of God] is more probable… στήκετε was changed… to… στήκητε… thanksgiving is always directed ‘to God’ rather than ‘to the Lord’… slightly stronger evidence for the inclusion of ἀμήν.”
- **Claim:** Weima adjudicates key variants: retain “boasting”; “coworker of God”; indicative stēkete; God not Lord in 3:9 thanksgivings; Amen in 3:13 as original-leaning.
- **Targets:** `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`, `timothy`, `1-thessalonians`
